subtype: Approach: only avoids bad outcomes and never defines a positive goal [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday: Raghav wrote his final-year plan as a list of things not to do: don't take a risky elective, don't join a busy club, don't apply anywhere he might not get in, don't pay for courses he might not finish. Preeti read it over his shoulder and said it looked safe.

Thursday: Raghav showed the plan to a senior and noticed that every line said what to avoid. No line said what he wanted. 'What are you aiming at?' asked Preeti. He couldn't say.

Following Monday: Raghav put down his pen. He had a plan that couldn't fail, and it also led nowhere. His week had been full of careful non-choices, and he still had no idea what he wanted to be doing in a year.

qa.q: What did every line of Raghav's plan say?
qa.a: Every line said what to avoid.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel when Preeti asked what he was aiming at?
qa.a: Raghav felt stuck and empty, since he couldn't answer and saw the plan pointed nowhere.

qa.q: What other step could Raghav take to build a real direction?
qa.a: Raghav could write down one thing he wants to be doing in a year and choose a small step toward it each month, keeping the avoid list as a side note.

qa.q: How might Preeti have seen the plan?
qa.a: Preeti probably saw a safe but empty plan, which is why Preeti said it looked safe and asked what Raghav was aiming at.

grounding: Shows a student who avoids every mistake he can think of, ending with a safe, empty plan and no positive goal.

passage:
Noor, you asked why I'm always telling you to aim at something. Let your Yogesh Nana tell you about his twenties.
At college I was afraid of mistakes. So I made a list of things never to do: never borrow, never take a risky course, never speak first in class, never apply where I might be rejected. I followed every rule perfectly.
Final year came. My friends had plans, a job they wanted, a subject they loved. I had no failures at all. And nothing else either. No project I cared about, no job I'd tried for, because trying meant risk.
I took the first safe clerk job that came. It took me seven years to leave it.
Avoiding the pothole is good, beti. But you also have to know where the road is going.

qa.q: How long did it take Yogesh to leave the clerk job?
qa.a: It took him seven years to leave it.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel in final year when his friends had plans?
qa.a: He felt empty and a little lost, since he had avoided every failure but had nothing he actually wanted.

qa.q: When Yogesh wrote the list of things never to do, what could he have added, and why?
qa.a: He could have added one thing to aim for, like a job or subject he loved, so the rules protected a goal instead of replacing it.

qa.q: How might Yogesh's friends have seen his careful college years?
qa.a: His friends may have seen him as steady but stuck, never trying for anything while they worked toward jobs and subjects they loved.

grounding: It shows a young man who avoids every mistake he can think of ending up with a safe but empty plan, since avoiding failure is not a goal.

passage:
The internship portal closed at midnight, and Pradeep's hostel Wi-Fi kept dropping. He had one hour to finalise his summer plan.
He opened the document he'd been polishing for weeks. It was titled "Things to avoid". No unpaid internships. Nothing far from home. No companies with bad reviews. Nothing that needed coding, since he'd failed a coding test once. Nothing with a long application.
He scrolled the list of internships. Every single one broke at least one rule, except a data-entry role at a local office.
His friend Swati messaged: "What are you applying for?"
Pradeep stared at the screen. "Data entry. It's safe."
"Is that what you want?"
He didn't reply. At 11.58 he submitted it, then sat back feeling strangely hollow. He had avoided every risk and chosen nothing he wanted.

qa.q: What was the one role that broke none of Pradeep's rules?
qa.a: A data-entry role at a local office.

qa.q: How did Pradeep feel after submitting at 11.58?
qa.a: He felt strangely hollow, since he had avoided every risk but chosen nothing he wanted.

qa.q: What would you change first in Pradeep's planning?
qa.a: I would start with one thing he wants to learn this summer, then use the avoid list only to rule out bad versions of that goal.

qa.q: How does Swati see Pradeep's choice?
qa.a: Swati seems doubtful, which is why Swati asks whether data entry is what he really wants.

grounding: It shows a student whose plan only lists things to avoid, ending with a safe but empty choice because no positive goal was set.
